messages.content: I want to design a mixed-criticality accelerator runtime. The goal is to guarantee control-task deadlines despite nonpreemptible inference kernels and shared-memory interference. Under declared execution and interference bounds, every admitted control job must meet its 2 ms deadline. Inference must also make starvation-free progress under adversarial arrivals, without compromising those control deadlines.

The runtime needs to satisfy two obligations at once. Its control guarantee applies to every admitted control job, under the declared execution and interference bounds: each must meet its 2 ms deadline. At the same time, adversarial arrivals must not let pending inference work be postponed indefinitely. Any account of the design has to address both the time spent behind a nonpreemptible inference kernel and the effects of shared-memory interference.
Why isn't it enough to give control jobs higher priority?

Priority does not interrupt a kernel that is already running and cannot be preempted. A control job could become ready while an inference kernel is in progress, so its deadline analysis cannot assume immediate access to the accelerator. Priority alone also does not establish how much shared-memory interference the control job may encounter.
So the nonpreemptible part matters even if the runtime always favors control whenever it gets to choose?

Yes. A favorable choice at the next opportunity cannot undo time already spent waiting for an in-progress, nonpreemptible kernel. To guarantee the admitted job's 2 ms deadline, the runtime has to account for that possible wait within the declared bounds, rather than treating control preference as instantaneous preemption.
Does the 2 ms requirement cover all control work that arrives?

It is stated for all *admitted control jobs*. That distinction matters: the requirement is not a claim that any amount of arriving control work can be accepted while retaining the deadline guarantee. Once a control job is admitted, though, the guarantee is that it meets its 2 ms deadline under the declared execution and interference bounds.
How should I think about those bounds without assuming particular hardware numbers?

They are the conditions under which the guarantee is made. The control-deadline argument needs to remain valid for execution and interference up to the declared bounds, including the consequences of nonpreemptible inference execution and shared-memory contention. The goal does not supply numerical values for those bounds or a particular way to calculate them.
Is shared-memory interference separate from waiting for a running inference kernel?

Conceptually, yes. Waiting for a nonpreemptible kernel concerns when a control job can begin using an occupied execution resource. Shared-memory interference concerns how contention can affect execution even when work is running. The deadline guarantee must account for both effects where they apply; considering only the initial wait would leave the interference part of the goal unaddressed.
What if execution or interference exceeds a declared bound?

The stated guarantee is conditional on the declared execution and interference bounds. It does not claim that the same 2 ms deadline guarantee holds when those conditions are exceeded. That does not say what the runtime would do in such a case; behavior beyond the bounds is not specified here.
And what does 'starvation-free inference progress' mean in this goal?

It means inference cannot be deferred forever merely because additional work keeps arriving. In particular, adversarial arrival timing must not create an endless pattern in which pending inference work never gets a chance to advance. This is a progress obligation, not a stated numerical inference deadline or throughput target.
Could a design meet the control deadline requirement just by never launching inference?

No. That might avoid one source of control blocking, but it would fail the separate requirement for starvation-free inference progress. The two requirements must hold together: inference must make progress under adversarial arrivals, and that progress must not compromise the 2 ms deadlines of admitted control jobs under the declared bounds.
Adversarial arrivals sound difficult. Does the goal mean the runtime must accept every control job and complete every inference request within a fixed time?

Neither claim is stated. The control deadline applies to admitted jobs, not necessarily every arriving job. For inference, starvation-free progress rules out indefinite postponement, but the goal gives no fixed completion-time bound. Adversarial arrivals are important because a steady stream of new work cannot, by itself, be allowed to defeat the inference-progress guarantee.
Is there a tension between always keeping control safe and ensuring inference moves forward?

Yes. Launching nonpreemptible inference work can affect when a control job can run, while withholding inference indefinitely would violate starvation freedom. A sound design has to identify opportunities for inference progress that remain compatible with the guarantee for admitted control jobs. If a claimed set of obligations demands more service than the resources can provide, that feasibility issue cannot be resolved by priority rules alone.
Would it be accurate to say that inference may proceed only when doing so cannot cause an admitted control deadline to be missed?

That captures the required safety relationship, provided 'cannot cause' is evaluated against the declared execution and interference bounds, not just the immediately visible workload. It also leaves the other half of the requirement intact: the runtime cannot invoke control safety as a reason to defer inference forever under adversarial arrivals.
Does starvation freedom require an inference kernel to be preemptible?

No. The goal explicitly includes nonpreemptible inference kernels. Starvation freedom concerns whether inference work gets to make progress despite competing arrivals; it does not require interrupting a kernel after it starts. Nonpreemptibility does, however, have to be accounted for when protecting admitted control jobs' 2 ms deadlines.
Can I claim a particular scheduling rule or a specific memory-management mechanism from this goal?

Not from the goal alone. It specifies what must be guaranteed and names two difficulties—nonpreemptible inference kernels and shared-memory interference—but does not choose a scheduling rule, a memory-management mechanism, or numerical bounds. Any such choice would need its own description and an argument that it satisfies both obligations.
Then what would a convincing argument for the runtime need to establish, at a high level?

It would need to show that admission and runtime behavior protect every admitted control job's 2 ms deadline for all execution and interference allowed by the declared bounds, including relevant nonpreemptible blocking and shared-memory effects. Separately, it would need to show that adversarial arrivals cannot indefinitely prevent inference progress. Crucially, the inference-progress argument cannot rely on behavior that breaks the control-deadline argument.
So neither a control-only timing argument nor an inference-only fairness argument is enough?

Right. A control-only argument could permit inference to starve, and a fairness argument in isolation could allow inference activity that makes an admitted control job miss its 2 ms deadline. The design goal requires the guarantees to coexist under the declared execution and interference bounds.

For the runtime, I propose admission-tested cyclic reservations, inference slices of at most 200 µs, bounded memory interference, 2 ms control response checks, and guaranteed inference slots. How do these pieces fit together?

The cyclic reservations provide a recurring structure for allocating accelerator time. Admission testing asks whether a proposed set of control jobs can meet its deadlines within that structure, using the declared execution and interference bounds. The ≤200-µs inference slices limit how long a slice of inference execution can occupy the accelerator without yielding an opportunity to run something else. The 2 ms response checks address the control requirement directly, while guaranteed inference slots reserve recurring opportunities for inference progress.
Why have both a slice limit and a control response check? Doesn't the 200 µs limit settle the deadline question?

Not by itself. A ≤200-µs inference slice bounds one source of nonpreemptible blocking, but a control job's response can also depend on its own execution, the reservation structure, other admitted work, and bounded shared-memory interference. The 2 ms check has to consider the relevant contributions together. A short inference slice is useful for that check; it is not a substitute for it.
Since the inference kernels are nonpreemptible, can a slice simply stop one at 200 µs?

No. A slice limit cannot make a nonpreemptible kernel interruptible. The proposal has to be applied so that the inference execution occupying a slice respects the ≤200-µs limit without assuming that a kernel can be stopped mid-execution. The proposal does not specify how inference work is arranged to satisfy that condition.
What does 'admission-tested' add to the cyclic reservations?

It makes acceptance of control work conditional on a deadline check rather than treating the recurring reservations as an automatic guarantee. For each admitted control job, the check must support a response within 2 ms under the declared execution and interference bounds, including the effects of inference execution allowed by the reservations. The proposal does not specify a particular admission-test formula.
Should that check assume the accelerator is free when a control job arrives?

No. That would overlook the nonpreemptible inference work the design is meant to handle. A sound 2 ms control response check needs to account for relevant blocking permitted by the reservation and slice rules, as well as the bounded interference. Otherwise admission could be based on a response time the runtime cannot actually guarantee.
How does bounded memory interference enter this proposal?

It is another part of the response-time conditions. Even with bounded inference slices, shared-memory contention can affect how long admitted control work takes. The control checks must include the declared bound on that interference where it applies. The proposal calls for bounded memory interference; it does not give a numerical bound or name a mechanism that enforces one.
And why make the reservations cyclic rather than just saying control has priority?

The cyclic structure makes room for recurring, guaranteed inference slots while still subjecting control admission to the 2 ms response checks. Priority alone would not say when inference must get service under adversarial arrivals. Here the intended combination is that inference has protected opportunities to run, but those opportunities are accounted for when deciding whether control work can be admitted with its deadline guarantee.
Does guaranteeing inference slots mean I can promise an inference completion deadline?

No inference completion deadline is stated. Guaranteed slots provide opportunities for inference progress; they do not, by themselves, specify how much work an inference request contains or a fixed time by which it finishes. The goal remains starvation-free inference progress under adversarial arrivals, without compromising admitted control deadlines.
Could adversarial control arrivals still fill every opportunity before inference gets one?

They must not defeat the guaranteed inference slots if the proposal is to satisfy its progress purpose. Control admission therefore has to be considered alongside those slots, rather than assuming inference receives whatever time happens to remain after accepting control work. At the same time, keeping the inference slots cannot be allowed to make an admitted control job miss its 2 ms deadline under the declared bounds.
Do guaranteed slots alone prove that no particular pending inference work starves?

Not necessarily. Slots establish that inference receives recurring service opportunities, but an argument about pending inference work also has to address how those opportunities translate into progress for that work under adversarial arrivals. This proposal names guaranteed slots without specifying the allocation policy among inference requests, so the slots are a key part of the starvation-freedom argument, not its entire proof.
Am I committing to a particular cycle length or a fixed number of inference slots?

No such values are given in the proposal. 'Cyclic reservations' and 'guaranteed inference slots' describe recurring allocation and protected inference opportunities, but they do not specify the cycle duration, the number of slots, or their placement. Any chosen arrangement would still have to pass the 2 ms control response checks and support starvation-free inference progress.
Is the 200 µs number the control deadline?

No. The two numbers serve different purposes: inference slices are limited to at most 200 µs, while admitted control jobs must meet 2 ms deadlines under the declared execution and interference bounds. The slice limit helps bound a source of delay in the control analysis; it does not replace or change the 2 ms deadline.
If a proposed reservation pattern fails a 2 ms response check, can I still use it because inference needs guaranteed slots?

Not while claiming the stated control guarantee for the jobs covered by that failed check. The point of admission testing is to avoid admitting control work whose 2 ms deadline cannot be established under the proposed reservations and bounds. The inference slots must be compatible with the control checks; neither requirement cancels the other.
Does passing a check mean the runtime has already demonstrated these guarantees in an experiment?

No experiment or result is part of this proposal. Admission-tested cyclic reservations are a proposed design approach. A passing check would be a conditional analytical basis for admitting work, provided its assumptions—including the execution, slice, and memory-interference bounds—hold. It should not be described as an observed result from information given here.

Let me restate it: reserve opportunities in a cycle for inference, constrain inference slices to ≤200 µs, and admit control only if its checked response meets 2 ms with bounded memory interference included. Is that the idea?

Yes. The intended design couples guaranteed inference opportunities with admission-tested protection for control. The check must cover the effects of the cyclic reservations, nonpreemptible inference execution within the ≤200-µs slice limit, and the declared memory-interference bound. It must establish the 2 ms deadline for every admitted control job, while the guaranteed inference slots contribute to starvation-free progress even under adversarial arrivals.
I should avoid saying that the slice cap alone proves either requirement, then?

Exactly. The ≤200-µs cap limits inference execution within a slice; it does not alone prove a 2 ms control response, and it does not alone guarantee that pending inference work gets served. Those claims depend on the admission-tested reservations, the bounded-interference assumptions, and an inference-progress argument that remains valid under adversarial arrivals.
How should the admission bounds account for kernel blocking and shared-memory contention while still guaranteeing inference slots under adversarial control releases?

The admission check should treat all three as parts of one worst-case control-response argument. It needs to account for a control job becoming ready while a nonpreemptible inference kernel is running, for the delay allowed by the cyclic reservations, and for the declared bound on shared-memory interference. It should check that every job it admits can still meet its 2 ms deadline while the guaranteed inference slots remain available, including when control releases occur at unfavorable times.
What is the right way to represent the kernel blocking in that check?

As a bound on how long a control job can be held up by inference execution that it cannot preempt, evaluated from an unfavorable arrival point. The proposed ≤200-µs inference slices are relevant to that bound, but the check must not assume it can interrupt a kernel at the slice boundary. It needs an execution bound consistent with the kernels actually being nonpreemptible and with the proposed slice limit.
So if control becomes ready just after an inference kernel begins, I should not count only the time until the next scheduling decision?

Correct. The relevant wait is until a decision can actually take effect. If the kernel remains nonpreemptible, a decision in favor of control cannot make the accelerator available sooner. The admission argument should cover that arrival timing, rather than assuming control always arrives at a convenient boundary.
Can I simply add 200 µs to every control job's response bound?

The ≤200-µs slice limit gives a candidate bound for an individual slice of inference execution, but simply adding that number is not automatically a complete or correctly counted response bound. The check has to establish what nonpreemptible execution a job could encounter under the reservations, whether any relevant delays can recur during its response, and how those delays relate to other terms in the bound. It should neither omit permitted blocking nor count the same delay twice.
What does shared-memory contention contribute if the kernel-blocking wait is already included?

Blocking accounts for time when the control job cannot proceed because nonpreemptible inference execution occupies what it needs. Shared-memory interference can affect the control job's execution time or other relevant parts of its response even apart from that wait. The admission check therefore needs a declared interference bound applicable to the control response it is checking, rather than treating the inference slice limit as a memory-contention bound.
Should I assume worst-case memory interference and worst-case blocking both occur?

The bound must cover any combination that is possible under the declared conditions. If both can affect one response, the check cannot quietly assume that only one occurs. Whether particular worst cases can overlap or must occur at different times depends on the model; the important point here is to form a safe total bound without relying on an unsupported separation or double-counting time that is already covered.
Would a response check that only considers the control job's own execution and one inference slice be sufficient?

Not on that description alone. It also needs to cover the effects of the cyclic reservations, other admitted control work where relevant, and the declared shared-memory interference bound. The question is whether the complete response of each admitted control job remains within 2 ms, not merely whether its own execution plus one possible wait looks small.
How do the guaranteed inference slots enter the control admission test?

They must be treated as part of the reservation structure that control has to tolerate. A control job should not pass admission only because the check silently assumes it can take time that is guaranteed to inference. The 2 ms response check has to succeed while accounting for those inference opportunities and the nonpreemptible work they permit.
What if a control job is released exactly when an inference slot is due?

That is the kind of unfavorable timing the admission bounds should address. The proposal cannot promise an inference slot and then assume it disappears whenever a control release coincides with it. Nor can it preserve the slot without checking its effect on the admitted control job's 2 ms response. The check needs to cover the allowed timing relationship between releases and slots.
Could I handle an adversarial burst by always handing inference slots over to control temporarily?

If repeated adversarial control releases can continually take every guaranteed inference opportunity, those slots no longer establish starvation-free inference progress. The proposal requires inference opportunities that remain meaningful under such releases. Control admission must be compatible with keeping them, rather than relying on indefinite displacement of inference whenever control is ready.
But if control arrivals are adversarial, how can any bound hold without knowing exactly when they'll arrive?

The check need not predict their exact times; it must cover the release patterns permitted by its declared assumptions, including unfavorable phasing. The 2 ms guarantee is for admitted control jobs under the declared execution and interference bounds. It is not a promise that every possible volume of control arrivals can be admitted. An admission rule has to avoid accepting work whose deadlines cannot be established while preserving the inference slots.
Does that mean the inference slots should be treated as unavailable to control during admission, even if they might sometimes be idle?

For a guarantee, the control check cannot depend on reclaiming time that inference is guaranteed to receive when it has pending work. Otherwise the check could pass only in the absence of the very inference activity it must coexist with. What to do with an unused opportunity is not specified here; the admission argument should remain valid when inference does use its guaranteed slots.
How do I avoid counting a slot and its inference kernel as two separate delays if they describe the same interval?

By making clear what each term in the response bound represents. A reservation term might describe when control is allowed to receive service, while a blocking term might describe a nonpreemptible kernel that is already in progress. If the same interval appears in both descriptions, the analysis needs to account for that relationship. The requirement is a safe bound on the complete response, not a particular arithmetic decomposition.
And I shouldn't assume the kernel always ends at a reservation boundary?

Right, not unless the proposed execution and reservation rules establish that. A nonpreemptible kernel cannot be forced to end merely because a boundary is reached. The relationship between the ≤200-µs slice limit, kernel execution bounds, and reservation boundaries has to be consistent for the admission check to use it safely.
How detailed does the memory-interference bound need to be?

Detailed enough that the 2 ms control response check can safely apply it to the contention the runtime permits. Saying only that memory interference exists would leave a gap in the bound; treating it as zero would also be unwarranted. This question does not supply a numerical bound or prescribe how it is obtained, only that the check must account for bounded shared-memory contention.
Does bounding contention for control automatically protect inference progress too?

Not automatically. A bound used to establish control response times addresses the control deadline argument. For inference progress, the runtime also needs inference opportunities that persist under adversarial control releases and an account of how pending inference work advances in those opportunities. Guaranteed slots help, but memory contention and any limits relevant to progress cannot simply be ignored in that separate argument.
Is the progress argument about the inference class as a whole or every pending inference request?

That distinction needs to be made explicit in a full starvation-freedom argument. Recurring slots can show that inference as a class is offered service, but they do not alone show that a particular pending request cannot be passed over forever. No allocation rule among inference requests is specified here, so the slot guarantee should not be overstated as a complete per-request proof.
Can the control response test and the inference-progress argument be done independently?

They address different properties, but they must use a consistent account of the same reservations and interference. The control test must include the cost of keeping inference slots; the progress argument must not depend on taking time away from admitted control jobs that their 2 ms checks require. Either argument would be incomplete if it assumed away the other's guaranteed service.
What should I say if a proposed set of control admissions only passes its response checks when the guaranteed inference slots are skipped?

Then those checks do not establish compatibility with this proposal. Admission has to be evaluated with the inference slots honored. If honoring them prevents establishing a 2 ms response for a control job, that job cannot be admitted on the strength of a check that assumes the slots are skipped.
Is there a concise way to state the admission obligation without choosing a cycle length or an interference value yet?

Yes: for every control job admitted under the declared execution, release, and interference assumptions, bound its worst-case response across the permitted cyclic reservations, including nonpreemptible inference blocking, shared-memory contention, and the guaranteed inference slots, and require that bound to meet its 2 ms deadline. Separately, establish that adversarial control releases cannot indefinitely prevent pending inference work from progressing through those slots. That states what the bounds must demonstrate without supplying unspecified cycle parameters or numerical interference values.

Here's a hypothesis for the admission bound: use a 200-µs inference reservation in every 2-ms frame, account for 200 µs of nonpreemptible blocking, and charge bounded memory stalls. Could that keep admitted control responses at or below 2 ms?

That is a candidate timing argument, not yet an established guarantee. The admission check would need to show that each admitted control job's full response is ≤2 ms under the declared bounds, with the per-frame inference reservation, possible 200-µs blocking, and applicable bounded memory-stall charges all represented correctly. The proposed numbers identify terms to examine; they do not by themselves prove the result.
What does the 200-µs inference reservation mean in this hypothesis?

It means setting aside 200 µs for inference in each 2-ms frame. For control admission, that reserved time cannot simply be treated as available whenever control needs it: the response check must remain valid when inference uses its reservation. For inference, the recurring reservation is intended to provide progress opportunities even when control releases are adversarial.
Is the 200-µs blocking term just another name for that reservation?

Not necessarily. The reservation describes time allocated to inference in the recurring frame; blocking describes a control job's wait behind an inference kernel it cannot preempt. Depending on the release time and how the reservation is modeled, those descriptions might cover some of the same elapsed time or different intervals. The admission calculation must make their relationship explicit rather than automatically adding them as independent charges or assuming one always subsumes the other.
Suppose a control job becomes ready while inference is running. Is that the case the blocking charge is meant to cover?

Yes. The proposed 200-µs blocking bound is meant to cover a possible wait for nonpreemptible inference execution. To use it safely, the runtime's permitted inference work would actually have to respect that bound; the scheduler cannot interrupt a nonpreemptible kernel merely because 200 µs have elapsed.
Does the inference reservation guarantee that blocking can never exceed 200 µs?

The reservation alone does not establish that. It specifies an allocation of time, whereas the blocking claim depends on the execution allowed within and around it. The hypothesis needs a consistent account of the nonpreemptible kernels and the ≤200-µs inference slices so that 200 µs is a defensible blocking bound, not just a number copied from the reservation length.
If a kernel reaches a frame boundary while still running, can the next frame force it to yield?

Not if it is nonpreemptible. A boundary has scheduling significance only when a running kernel can actually finish or yield in accordance with the proposed bounds. The hypothesis would need to account for any execution crossing a boundary; it cannot rely on the frame boundary itself to stop a kernel.
Would I check only jobs released at the start of a 2-ms frame?

No. A response bound for admitted control jobs needs to cover unfavorable release times, including releases during an inference reservation or while a nonpreemptible kernel is running. Checking only frame-aligned releases could miss blocking or reservation delay experienced at other phases.
Is a 2-ms frame automatically enough to ensure a 2 ms control response?

No. Frame duration and response deadline happen to have the same stated length here, but that equality is not a proof. A job's response depends on its release time, the service it can obtain, relevant admitted work, blocking, and memory stalls. The admission check must establish ≤2 ms for the complete response, rather than inferring it from the frame length.
Should I assume that a job's response stays within one frame?

Not without establishing that from the reservation and admission rules. A job released partway through a frame may have a response interval that reaches into the next one. The bound should cover the reservations and other delays that can fall within the whole response interval, wherever the frame boundaries occur.
How should I include the bounded memory-stall charges?

They should represent the shared-memory interference that can delay the admitted control job under the declared bound. The check needs to apply those charges wherever contention can affect its response, without treating them as zero and without counting the same elapsed interval twice. The hypothesis supplies no numerical memory-stall bound, so its sufficiency remains conditional on what is declared and enforced.
Could I say control meets 2 ms because the reservation and blocking are each only 200 µs?

That would leave out too much. Even if those two 200-µs quantities are valid, the full response also includes the control job's bounded execution, applicable memory stalls, and any other service delay permitted for admitted work. Moreover, the two quantities need to be related correctly in the timing analysis. The ≤2 ms conclusion has to follow from a complete admission check.
What if I count both 200-µs terms in every response, just to be safe?

Counting both may be conservative in some circumstances, but it should still have a clear meaning. If the reservation delay and kernel blocking describe the same interval, charging both could reject work unnecessarily; if they can arise separately, collapsing them into one could be unsafe. The hypothesis does not settle which case applies. The admission model has to identify what each term bounds for each possible release phase.
Can I reserve the inference time but let control take it whenever a control release is inconvenient?

If adversarial releases can repeatedly displace the inference reservation, it would not reliably guarantee inference opportunities. The hypothesis should be evaluated with the 200-µs inference reservation in each 2-ms frame honored, including inconvenient control-release times. Control admission then has to establish the ≤2 ms response bound in the presence of that reserved inference time.
Does one reservation in each frame prove starvation freedom for inference?

It supplies recurring opportunities for inference as a class, which is relevant to progress under adversarial control releases. By itself, it does not show that every particular pending inference request advances: that also depends on how the reserved opportunities are assigned among pending inference work and whether work can make progress within the declared bounds. The reservation is part of the hypothesis, not a complete starvation-freedom proof.
Is the admission decision where the control and inference requirements meet?

Yes. A control job should be admitted only if its response can be bounded by 2 ms while the recurring inference reservations are retained and the declared blocking and memory-stall bounds are respected. The check cannot obtain a passing control result by assuming away inference service, because the design also requires inference progress under adversarial arrivals.
What if the bounded memory stalls turn out larger than the response check allows?

Then that check would not establish the hypothesized ≤2 ms response under those stalls. The claim is conditional on the declared interference bound and on the admission test incorporating it. This hypothesis does not give a measured stall value or show which sets of jobs would pass.
Should the blocking term be applied to inference only, or is it a general estimate of all delay?

Here, the proposed 200-µs blocking term refers specifically to waiting behind nonpreemptible inference execution. It should not stand in for shared-memory stalls or for every effect of the cyclic reservation. Keeping those effects distinct makes it possible to check whether the complete response bound is sound.
Could the recurring reservations and blocking matter more than once during a response?

That depends on the permitted timing and how the response interval intersects the frames. The check should account for whatever reservation time and nonpreemptible execution can actually delay the job over its full response, rather than assuming without justification that a single charge always suffices or that every possible charge necessarily accumulates. Unfavorable release phasing is important to that determination.
How should I phrase the hypothesis without sounding as though it has already been proved?

You could say: 'Hypothesis: reserving 200 µs for inference in every 2-ms frame, bounding nonpreemptible inference blocking at 200 µs, and charging bounded shared-memory stalls allows admission checks to keep every admitted control response at ≤2 ms while preserving inference opportunities under adversarial control releases.' That states the proposed relationship while leaving its verification open.
And the key test is whether those charges really cover every admitted job, even at an unfavorable release time?

Yes. The hypothesis stands or falls on a sound full-response bound: it must cover the relevant frame phasing, actual nonpreemptible blocking, memory stalls, and admitted work while keeping the inference reservations in place. Until that has been established, ≤2 ms for admitted control jobs and starvation-free inference progress remain intended outcomes of the proposal, not demonstrated results.

I want to turn the reservation-and-blocking hypothesis into a plan: derive admission inequalities from its reservation, blocking, and memory-stall bounds, implement the scheduler, and stress-test both control deadlines and inference progress. How should I keep those steps connected?

Use the same timing assumptions throughout. First derive inequalities that admit a control job only when its bounded response meets the 2 ms deadline while the proposed inference reservations remain in place. Then implement scheduling behavior consistent with the reservation and blocking assumptions used in those inequalities. Finally, stress-test whether control deadlines and inference progress behave as intended, including under adversarial arrivals. Those tests can expose problems, but they do not replace the conditional admission argument.
What should the admission inequalities actually bound?

They should bound the complete response of each control job being considered for admission, not just its execution on the accelerator. The derivation needs to account for the hypothesized inference reservations, delay behind nonpreemptible inference execution, and the declared memory-stall charges, along with other admitted control work where relevant. Admission should require the resulting bound to be no greater than 2 ms.
Should I start by adding a reservation charge, a blocking charge, and a memory-stall charge?

Those are the proposed ingredients, but the derivation must define what interval each charge covers before combining them. Reservation delay and nonpreemptible blocking might describe overlapping time, or they might arise separately for some release timings. The inequality must cover every permitted response without omitting a delay or counting an interval twice merely because it has two names.
Does the plan assume the hypothesis is already correct?

No. Deriving the inequalities is one way to examine whether the hypothesized bounds can support the claimed response limit. If an assumed bound is not justified, or the complete response cannot be shown to fit within 2 ms while retaining inference reservations, the proposed admission argument would need further work. Implementation and stress tests are planned steps, not completed validation.
How do the proposed 200-µs inference reservations in every 2-ms frame enter the derivation?

They are time the control-response check must account for when inference uses it. A job's release might occur at an unfavorable point relative to a frame, so the derivation should consider how the recurring reservation can affect its full response interval. It must not obtain a passing inequality by treating the guaranteed inference time as free control capacity.
And the hypothesized 200-µs blocking bound?

That is intended to bound waiting behind a nonpreemptible inference kernel. Before using it in an inequality, the plan needs to establish that permitted inference execution really obeys that bound, including at reservation boundaries. The scheduler cannot rely on preempting a kernel to make an assumed 200-µs blocking limit true.
Where do the bounded memory stalls fit?

They belong in the control-response bound wherever shared-memory interference can extend that response under the declared conditions. The derivation should make the charge applicable to the interference the implementation permits. Since no numerical memory-stall bound has been given, the plan is to derive the inequality using a declared bound, not to claim a particular workload already passes it.
Do I need to consider releases that do not line up with the 2-ms frames?

Yes. The admission inequalities should cover unfavorable release phases, including a control job becoming ready during an inference reservation or while a nonpreemptible kernel is running. Restricting the derivation to frame-aligned releases would not establish the deadline for every admitted control job.
Would meeting the inequality for an individual job be enough to admit it?

Only if the inequality accounts for the admitted workload it must coexist with. The plan is to derive admission conditions for control responses under the declared bounds and the maintained inference reservations, not to check each job in isolation while ignoring other admitted work that could affect its response.
What is the scheduler implementation supposed to demonstrate?

It is supposed to realize the behavior assumed by the admission analysis: the cyclic inference reservations, the conditions underlying the nonpreemptible blocking bound, and the treatment of control work on which the response check relies. It also has to preserve inference opportunities despite adversarial control releases. The plan does not yet specify implementation details or establish that an implementation achieves these properties.
If the implementation sometimes lets control use an inference reservation, is that necessarily incompatible with the plan?

The essential question is whether the scheduler still guarantees the inference opportunities on which the progress argument relies and whether its behavior matches the admission inequalities. The plan does not specify a rule for unused reservation time. It cannot, however, depend on repeatedly displacing pending inference work whenever control arrives and still call those opportunities guaranteed under adversarial releases.
What should the stress tests look for on the control side?

They should look for missed 2 ms deadlines among admitted control jobs, particularly with timing that exercises reservation delays, nonpreemptible blocking, and shared-memory interference. They should also check whether observed scheduler behavior respects the assumptions used for admission. A stress test can reveal a violation; observing no violations in a test does not prove the bound for every arrival pattern allowed by the model.
What should they look for on the inference side?

They should look for whether inference actually advances when control releases are arranged to be unfavorable, rather than receiving slots only when control happens to be quiet. Because starvation freedom concerns pending inference work, the tests should also examine whether recurring opportunities translate into progress instead of merely showing that the inference class is allocated time. No specific test outcome is implied by the plan.
Could I claim starvation freedom if stress tests show inference received some time?

Not on that observation alone. Some inference service in a finite test does not establish that adversarial arrivals cannot postpone pending work indefinitely. The progress argument needs to explain why the scheduler keeps providing meaningful opportunities and how pending inference work can advance through them. Stress tests can challenge that argument and identify counterexamples.
